html:
When we pour water into a glass, we often notice that the pitch of the sound keeps rising from low to high. A good deal of acoustics lies behind this everyday phenomenon. Studies show that as a container is filled with water, you can hear the sound glide gradually from a low tone to a high one.

Understanding the effect not only reveals the physics of air-column and container resonance; it also makes a good demonstration for acoustics experiments and teaching. As one science program pointed out, the pitch reaches its highest as a wine bottle or glass fills up, because the container acts as a Helmholtz resonator.

Sound is a wave of mechanical vibration traveling through a medium. Its basic properties include frequency (which determines pitch) and amplitude (which determines loudness). In air, sound travels at about c ≈ 343 m/s, and its wavelength λ and frequency f are related by c = f · λ. When sound passes between different media, such as air and water, the difference in acoustic impedance reflects most of the sound energy. The acoustic impedances of air and water differ by a factor of about 3,600, so a sound wave traveling from air onto a water surface is almost totally reflected: only about 0.1% of the energy is transmitted. The water surface in a glass can therefore be treated as a “closed end” for airborne sound, which profoundly changes how the air column vibrates.

An air column closed at one end has characteristic resonance frequencies. For a container that is open at the top, the air-column resonance can be approximated by a closed-tube model or by a Helmholtz resonator.

The resonance frequency is thus inversely proportional to the length L of the air column: as the air column gets shorter, the resonance frequency rises.

Bubbles oscillating in a liquid also make sound. As early as 1921, Bragg pointed out that the sound of running water comes mainly from the formation and bursting of bubbles, and later research has broadly agreed that bubble formation is the main source of sound in liquids. The natural resonance frequency of a single bubble is inversely proportional to its radius: the larger the bubble, the lower its frequency. The bubbles formed while pouring, whose size depends on the flow rate and the properties of the liquid, therefore also shape the sound.

In practice, the pitch of water being poured into a glass rises steadily. In experiments, for instance, the measured resonance frequency rises markedly as the glass goes from nearly empty to nearly full, consistent with the higher frequency of a shorter air column. The reasons can be summarized as follows:

  • The resonator changes size: as the water level rises, the length L of the remaining air column keeps shrinking. According to the air-column resonance formula, the resonance frequency is inversely proportional to the length of the air column. So as you pour, the volume of air in the container shrinks, the natural frequency of the resonant cavity gradually rises, and the pitch rises with it.

  • Reflection at the water–air interface: the high acoustic impedance of the water surface reflects airborne sound almost completely. The air column is open at the top and behaves as a closed, rigid end at the water surface (strong reflection), forming the resonance of a tube closed at one end. A rising water level is equivalent to shortening this closed tube, which raises its resonance frequency.

  • Vibration of the container: the walls and body of the glass have natural frequencies of their own. Experiments show that when glasses filled to different levels are tapped, the more water a glass holds, the lower its vibration frequency, because the extra water adds mass and damping to the vibrating system and lowers its natural frequency. While pouring, the high tone produced purely by the air column therefore stands out more, while the structural vibration of the container is pushed down and gradually dies away.

Several other factors also affect how the sound changes as you pour:

  • Pouring speed: the faster the flow, the harder the water strikes, and the larger the droplets and bubbles it usually forms. Since large bubbles resonate at lower frequencies, fast pouring with vigorous bubble formation adds lower-frequency noise components. A strong stream can also change the air column more abruptly, so the pitch changes at a different rate.

  • Water temperature and viscosity: temperature affects the viscosity and surface tension of water. Hot water is less viscous and flows more freely, so the stream breaks up more readily into fine droplets and tiny bubbles; cold water is more viscous and tends to form larger droplets and bubbles. Pouring hot water therefore produces small bubbles with higher resonance frequencies and a crisper sound, while cold water produces large bubbles with lower frequencies and a lower pitch. Experiments have also found that the liquid level, viscosity and temperature are negatively correlated with the container’s resonance frequency: the more water, the higher the viscosity or the lower the temperature, the lower the resonance frequency.

  • Material and shape of the glass: glasses of different materials and shapes also sound different. The elastic modulus and density of the material determine the natural frequencies of the walls, and stiffer materials generally have higher natural frequencies. The shape of the glass (the size of the mouth, the wall thickness, its symmetry and so on) affects both the air-column modes and the structural vibration modes. Studies show that wine glasses of different sizes respond with different sensitivity to changes in water level and temperature, which shows that the size and shape of a container change its resonance conditions. In general, a container with a narrow neck behaves more like an ideal Helmholtz resonator and its change in pitch is more pronounced, while a wide, shallow glass may combine several resonance modes, making the change in sound more complex.

The changing sound you hear while pouring water comes mainly from the air-column resonance frequency shifting with the water level. As water goes in, the remaining air column gets shorter, so its resonance frequency rises, and we hear the pitch climb from low to high. At the same time, the high-impedance reflection at the water–air interface strengthens the air-column vibration, while the container’s own vibration is damped by the mass of the water, which further brings out the air-column resonance. This acoustic analysis agrees closely with experimental observation and confirms that resonance theory applies to everyday phenomena. Understanding the process not only explains the familiar sound of pouring water but also gives acoustics a tangible example, a neat meeting of theory and the real world.
